Date: May 2, 1955 From: Vavilov Archivist M. Orlikova To: Club President P. Savelyeva  I just got a REALLY weird message, Polina. Remember when Arkady raised that bull on Polymer-based food? You know, the one named Hercules who was as big as a house? It was in the papers and everything. Anyway, some pictures of the bull somehow got leaked abroad and made their way to—GET THIS—some Spanish cattle breeders. Yeah, I'm serious—Spanish. Cattle. Breeders. To make a long story short, they want to order a few of our bovine behemoths for their "corrida" or whatever they call it. You know, bullfighting. International friendship and all that. I didn't know who to talk to about this, or even what to think... but I dunno, maybe the bosses will take an interest in it.  I'm still in shock.
Date: May 2, 1955 From: V. Neyelov To: A. Neyelova  I'm leaving right away on the first train, honey. Hang on and be strong. Yours, Vlad
Date: May 2, 1955 From: Junior Radiophysicist I. Shniperson To: Junior Radiophysicist S. Pestsov  We did it, Sergey! Listen!

Date: May 2, 1955 From: Senior Research Assistant Y. Notov To: Academy of Consequences Archive  A fundamental distinction  We are waiting for signals from outer space and bombarding infinity with powerful pulses, like we're standing in a dark forest shouting "anybody there?!" Even a scientist's brilliant mind that fully comprehends the vastness of space finds it inconceivable that nowhere in the potentially infinite expanses of the Universe there's anyone else endowed with intelligence. But what if we don't find anyone to talk to in this "dark forest" just because we don't share a common language? I'm not just talking about human language, of course. Imagine what would happen if we encountered a life form that was, for example, literally unfamiliar with mathematics, and its overall paradigm had no place for a similar system. How could we possibly communicate with a species like that? That brings me to a question: how many times could we already have encountered something that we simply failed to acknowledge as another life form?

Date: May 2, 1955 From: Senior Research Assistant Y. Notov To: Secretary A. Chubakov  The Ministry of Defense has requested clarification regarding the signals from outer space. Apparently the fad for alien-related pranks has now gotten its claws into even the brainiest of us thanks to Orson Wells's little escapade. I've sketched out a report for them. I'd like you to draw it up in those simple, gloomy terms military men appreciate and send it over to them. We currently have five working theories regarding the repeating signals from space.  Neutron star When a star goes nova and dies, it can transform into a quickly revolving neutron star. We believe that neutron stars within a strong magnetic field could emit similar strange signals.  A merging of two stars Another potential explanation is the collision of two neutron stars. Most radio bursts detected by telescopes over the last decade have been singular.  Blitzar A quickly revolving neutron star that cannot bear its own weight, so it collapses very quickly and transforms into a black hole.   Black hole There is a theory that radio bursts can be emitted by a neutron star falling into a black hole. Or the black hole itself could emit them as it quickly shrinks. Or dark matter could do the same as it collides with a black hole.  Human error The imperfections inherent in available equipment (even Soviet equipment), human error when calculating data—either of these things could lead to an inaccurate interpretation.

Date: May 2, 1955 From: Robo-Theater Director S. Lastochkin To: #robo-theater  Comrades, we have been ordered to put on an unforgettable performance in six weeks to celebrate the launch of the neural network. It's a very important event, and the show needs to take people's breath away. If you have any trouble with the robots, call Viktor. He isn't Petrov but he's pretty helpful too.  And there's more! Man has now been to space, and the Party wants a performance on a space-related theme. Get started as soon as possible.   And let's plan the concert for Vavilov Complex toward the end of the summer. Something related to cultivation. They've got some achievements to celebrate there, something about bullrushes or hemlock or something. Anyway, we'll worry about that later, but keep it in mind.

Date: September 2, 1953 From: Junior Research Assistant S. Pestsov To: #down_with#Sechenov  Comrades! I would like to invite all interested persons to sign a petition to change the name of our scientific center back to Popov. Everyone knows that, thanks to Comrade Sechenov, our radio antennas can hearken to the frigid breath of outer space, but it's thanks to Comrade Popov that those antennas exist in the first place! Space is great and all, but what if there's actually nothing out there? Join me, comrades!

Date: February 2, 1955 From: Robo-Theater Director S. Lastochkin To: Office Manager F. Surkov  Day in, day out, it's the same thing! Update the firmware on the coat check girl already, Comrade Surkov! What's going on with her? She's supposed to take people's coats, give them tickets, and sew loops, not greet guests by dancing right in the foyer! People just blush and look away! This is a Soviet theater, not a beer hall! She's just a robotic clothes hanger, not a performer! I'm holding you personally responsible for her behavior! P.S. And yes, I know that Vasily the electrician is "in love" with her and is always hovering around here. I don't give a damn about his tastes, but he's scaring the guests away with his appearance! Handle this!

Date: April 21, 1955  From: V. Neyelov To: Graduate Student A. Neyelova  Dear Annie,  Unfortunately, I'm going to be on the duty for another six months. But can you imagine how great it's going to be when they launch KOLLEKTIV? No more letters, phones, or telegrams! You and I will always be in touch! I'm in Kamchatka, but you'll be able to read me poetry and tell me about what your new species of apple smells like. I can't wait. Until then, I'll just kiss this letter. By which I mean the screen. Well, not really... you get it ;)  Yours always, your husband Vladimir

Seriously, no more crazy Malevich-type stuff, okay? Here are the quotes:  "Nature isn't a temple, it's a workshop, and in it, man is the worker." I. Turgenev.  "Apple trees will bloom on Mars too!" E. Dolmatovsky  "We can't expect handouts from nature. We need to take them from her." E. Michurin  "Robots serve man, and man serves society." D. Sechenov  "Turn the lights out when leaving."  "Respect the janitor."  "When leaving your workplace, put the key in the safe."

There are so many of them, and I'm just one man. My team of buffoons don't count—they're worthless as doctors. Let's do this: I'll take the most interesting cases, and hopefully Kollektiv 2.0 can treat the rest of them.

He will be here with VIPs in two weeks. The robots need to perform flawlessly. We have made a major breakthrough in international relations, and the celebration has to blow them away. Bring out your best ballerinas, add a few beautiful performers, and offer them a magnificent banquet. You wanted to come up with a new show—well, this is your chance. Make it something about robots and atomic power. I'm counting on you! P.S. And get rid of that monstrosity with the bow! She's giving people nightmares—even the war veterans!
Date: March 24, 1955 From: Junior Radiophysicist S. Pestsov To: Senior Research Assistant Y. Notov  I found it, Yevgeny! I found it! Listen, here it is! Eureka! It's a real message!

Date: May 25, 1955 From: Junior Radiophysicist I. Schnipperson To: Senior Research Assistant Y. Notov  I, Isaac Schnipperson, on May 23rd, between 11:04 and 11:56 PM local time, independently and without authorization, used my professional position and equipment to hack into the control system of a dual-purpose satellite belonging to the United States of America. While controlling the aforementioned satellite, I altered its trajectory in order to display text of an offensive and indecent nature via its flight path as depicted on the center's screens. I affirm that I am now aware that political conflicts and ideological dissent between nations cannot serve as a justification for such unprofessional behavior, and I sincerely regret having inconvenienced my colleagues in the US. I apologize for my actions, admit my wrongdoing, and accept disciplinary action.

Date: February 28, 1953 From: DATA DELETED To: Office Manager S. Date: April 29, 1955.  I hasten to inform you that Stefan Lastochkin, the manager of the theater, entered the greenhouse without authorization yesterday and asked us to grow a rose for his personal needs. He requested that it be "an exceptionally beautiful rose unlike any other in the world, and it should be called Maya, after Maya Plisetskaya." This is all very sweet, of course, but I demand that you explain to Comrade Lastochkin that the modeling department is not a flower shop, but a serious laboratory! We appreciate beauty as much as the next person, but we're trying to conquer new worlds here, not delight ballerinas with pretty bouquets!

Date: May 29, 1955 From: Senior Diagnostician G. Haus To: Head Physician K. Lizova  Klavdia, the patients Pavlov has been sending us... even my professional intellect flinches in horror and doesn't want to deal with them.  Autopsies have been showing more and more brutal torture. And there are more of these people every day! At this rate Kollektiv 2.0 won't have anyone to enlighten. All that's left will be flabby, freakish corpses—just the kind you love, my treasure. Figure out what we're going to do about this, since you're the head physician. In the meantime, I'll go back to my patients, since I'm a brilliant diagnostician.

Date: June 3, 1955 From: #maglev #station_master P. Stamatin To: Breeder U. Kopylov  In case you don't remember, the Lesnaya Maglev train station is on the outskirts of our village. It's one of the most important transportation hubs in the entire Facility and the greatest achievement of the Soviet Union. So why am I bringing it up? The day before yesterday one of your cows walked out onto the "track" (or a "line"). Do you have any idea what a collision like that would do to the Maglev train?  Nothing at all, actually. But unless you want your animals to get ground into chuck, I suggest keeping an eye on them. Put trackers on them or something. Thanks in advance.

Date: March 3, 1953 From: Office Manager S. Lastochkin To: Maya Plisetskaya Theater Artistic Director A. Lyubin  Comrade Lyubin, I sincerely regret that you still don't approve of my idea. And I also regret that the theater is run by such a narrow-minded twit. My "backstage" is a litmus test for the virtue of outstanding Soviet citizens! Did you really think it was just a regular old brothel?! I'll have you know that Comrade Stockhausen and I have much greater plans for it! And if you're foolish enough to go to him with your evidence, here's a little more "evidence" for you!  *attachment: photo of a woman's chest

You'll be closely studying signals from outer space and trying to determine which, if any, could lead to the discovery of non-terrestrial civilizations. There is top secret information available suggesting that we ought to keep looking. I've got high hopes for you. Your new assignment is effective immediately.

Shniperson  Comrade Shniperson, Thank you for the message about your vital discovery regarding the potential radio-free transmission of a signal via the vibrational structure of the Polymer. Date: December 7, 1954 From: Facility 3826 Deputy Director M. Stockhausen To: Robotics Workshop Senior Research Assistant V. Petrov  I must admit, Viktor, you are talented! People can say what they will about your... idiosyncrasies, shall we call them, but your skills are undeniable. Your work with the neural network and robots... you could write textbooks about it. I'd never noticed your abilities before. What's your secret? Is your new paramour giving you some additional motivation?  But that's none of my concern. I've got good news: I've gotten you quite the promotion! We'll celebrate your lofty new position as soon as you configure the new Neuropolymers from Pavlov for data exchange. I owe you a mug of your favorite Bavarian beer!

Send your observers to eliminate the remnants of the Neyelov experiment, Comrade Bur.
